_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 1 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 2 Order Matters. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (socks and shoes; a sandwich in order; a bug; fixing it; changing the outcome), then the lesson's own crossing-the-road step for 1CT.04, in the lesson's own words. Every wrong order is drawn by passing the WRONG LIST to the lesson's own scene - ART.scene(dress, [shoes, socks]) and ART.scene(sandwich, [bread, butter, top, jam]) - so the kit labels its own consequence and the film draws no picture of a mistake.
title: Order Matters
subtitle: Grade 1 Computing
objectives: Know that the order of instructions is important when creating algorithms.
Identify single errors in algorithms that represent everyday events or tasks.
Suggest ways that algorithms can be changed to affect the outcome.
Follow the steps in algorithms for everyday tasks.
Suggest sets of ordered instructions to complete simple tasks, such as drawing a picture of a particular object or building a brick tower.

beats.say: Put on your socks, then your shoes. Now try it the other way round.
Same two steps, a different order, and a very silly outcome.
Sami is getting dressed. The algorithm has two steps: socks, then shoes.
Follow it in that order, and Sami is ready to go outside.
Now swap the two steps round. Shoes first, then socks.
Oh no! The socks are on the outside of the shoes.

at.outside: on the outside of the shoes

beats.say: Same two steps. A different order. A different outcome.
A jam sandwich is an algorithm too. It has four steps to follow.
Bread on the plate. Then butter on the bread.
Then jam on the butter, and the top slice on the jam.

at.top: the top slice on the jam

beats.say: Every step has its place. Now put the top slice on before the jam.
The jam ends up on the outside of the sandwich, and on your fingers.
A mistake in an algorithm is called a bug.
Read this one. Bread. Pour milk on the bread. Jam. Top slice.
Milk does not belong in a jam sandwich. That step is the bug.
A bug can also be a right step that sits in the wrong place.
The top slice before the jam is one of those. Finding the bug comes first.

at.top: The top slice before the jam

beats.say: When you have found the bug, the next job is to fix it.
Take the wrong step out, and put the right step in.
The milk step goes out. The butter step goes in.
Or take that early top slice and move it to where it belongs.
Then run the algorithm again and check. A jam sandwich!
You can change an algorithm on purpose, to make something new.
Swap the jam step for cheese, and you get a cheese sandwich.

at.swap: Swap the jam step for cheese

beats.say: Add a step at the end, cut it in half, and you get two halves.

at.add: Add a step at the end

beats.say: The steps decide what you get. What you get is the outcome.
Change a step, and you change the outcome.
Some algorithms keep you safe. Then the order really matters.
Crossing the road has four steps, and you can put them in order.
Stop at the kerb. Look both ways. Listen for cars. Then walk across.
Walk first and you are already in the road. Stop, look, listen, walk.
The same steps in a different order do a different thing.
A bug is a mistake in the steps. Find it, and then fix it.
Change one step, and the outcome changes too.
